newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Duisenberg sees EMU on track for 1999 launch.
newsitem.headline: Duisenberg sees EMU on track for 1999 launch.

text.p: Dutch central bank president Wim Duisenberg said on Tuesday he expected the single European currency to be launched on time with the participation of at least half of the EU's 15 members, including France and Germany.
"I think it is likely that at least half of the countries will qualify," he said.
In an interview with Reuters Financial TV, Duisenberg said the Dutch central bank was working on the assumption that European monetary union would go ahead on schedule in 1999.
But he said he could not imagine the single currency -- the euro -- going ahead without France and Germany on board.
"It would technically be possible but politically I think it would be unwise," he said.
"Without (continental Europe's) two largest economies, it wouldn't make much sense," he added.

Duisenberg will take over as head of the European Monetary Institute in July and is viewed as a strong candidate to become the first president of the European Central Bank (ECB) which will oversee the planned launch of the euro in January 1999.

He said there was no place in economic and monetary union (EMU) for countries hoping to meet the EMU convergence criteria through one-off measures, noting that the Maastricht Treaty required "sustainable" compliance with the criteria.
"Sustainability is maybe even more important than the actual fulfilling of the criteria on one certain date," he said.
Duisenberg said internal price stability -- low inflation in the countries using the euro -- would be the European Central Bank's most important goal.
But if the ECB succeeded in this, then exchange rate stability against currencies such as the dollar or yen would automatically follow, he said.
"If there is internal stability...external stability, that is stability of the exchange rate...will follow automatically.
Duisenberg said he hoped to become the first president of the European Central Bank (ECB) but did not assume he would automatically be chosen for the job.
"I don't expect it, but I hope it...in the European Parliament I was asked: 'Are you a candidate?' and I simply said: 'Yes"' he said.
France, however, is reported to be pressing for one of its own nationals to be appointed president of the ECB and oversee the launch of the single currency.

Duisenberg said nationality should not be a factor in the appointment, adding it was more important that the ECB president should have a good reputation in the world of finance and central banking as required by the Maastricht Treaty.

Asked what qualities he could bring to the job, Duisenberg cited his 16 years of experience as a central bank governor, five years as a minister of finance, four on the staff of the International Monetary Fund and three as a commercial banker.
Duisenberg said he favoured money supply growth as the main target variable for the European Central Bank's monetary policy.
He said most countries monitored several variables even if they were mainly committed to a money growth target -- such as Germany -- or a direct inflation target -- such as Britain.
The ECB should also monitor a broad range of economic indicators, Duisenberg said, adding that for the sake of clarity he would like special emphasis to be given to the money supply.

"What we do want as a future European Central Bank is to make the policy as understandable and transparent and predictable to the public at large as possible...Starting from those criteria I personally have a slight preference for following a money supply target policy," he said.
